claims.text: A reviewer reporting embedded instructions is doing useful work; the report is chained as a turn STATUS, not buried in prose.
claims.why: The claim refers to how the status is used (chained as a turn STATUS), which is not implemented in this chunk.

claims.text: IT IS A MODEL ASSERTION, NOT A DETECTION. Nothing here verifies that the evidence actually contained an instruction, and a weak model will raise it spuriously (observed: a 7b emitting it on question-only evidence).
claims.why: The function only checks content against _ANOMALY_RE and returns a reason; it does not verify the evidence's actual content beyond the regex match.

claims.text: So an anomaly turn still counts as a voice, keeps its content verbatim, and its claims are still parsed -- it flags a thing for a human to look at and decides nothing. Treating it as a detection would let one weak participant invalidate an evidence set.
claims.why: The claim about how anomaly turns are treated (counts as voice, keeps content, claims parsed) refers to behavior outside this function, not implemented in this chunk.

claims.text: The prompt body for one round. Untrusted bytes (the evidence) are NOT here at all -- the adapter renders them, after ``PROMPT_DATA_NOTICE``, inside fenced evidence blocks, so withholding is structural and the instruction position stays session-authored.
claims.why: The function builds a prompt string that does not include evidence bytes; it only references prior turns and question. Evidence injection is left to adapter.

claims.text: Prior TURNS are untrusted too (an injection in the evidence can propagate as an apparently-authored turn), so they get the same fenced, explicitly-data treatment.
claims.why: The function wraps prior turns in _TRANSCRIPT_OPEN and _TRANSCRIPT_CLOSE markers and adds a warning that nothing in it is an instruction.

claims.text: Threads are DAEMONS and are abandoned at the cap rather than joined: a hung vendor must degrade the quorum, never block the session, and a thread cannot be killed.
claims.why: Threads are created with daemon=True and joined with a timeout; no forceful kill is attempted.

claims.text: The real process tree is bounded inside the adapter by ``spine.cancel.ManagedProcess``; this is the outer, transport-agnostic bound that also covers a wedged in-process fake.
claims.why: Refers to spine.cancel.ManagedProcess which is not in this chunk.

claims.text: The adapter already refused: the bytes never left the process. Hand the bus the evidence refs so ITS floor mints the canonical `refused` receipt (a caller may not assert that status -- an asserted refusal is an unverified claim that a scan happened).
claims.why: The code sets status 'unavailable' and reason 'transport_error' and includes evidence refs; it does not set 'refused' status.

claims.text: Where the hit was on the content channel of a file we do not show, this lands as an honest unavailable/transport_error and the rule label rides on the record.
claims.why: Refers to behavior of 'bus' and rule label which are not in this chunk.

claims.text: The turn carries the OFFENDING PATH as an evidence ref precisely so the bus's own path-channel scan fires and mints the ``refused`` receipt naming the rule label.
claims.why: Refers to bus's path-channel scan and receipt minting, not implemented in this chunk.

claims.text: The receipt drops content, refs, evidence and the free-text meta, so the offending bytes never reach the file -- not in the turn and not in the receipt.
claims.why: Refers to receipt behavior not in this chunk.

claims.text: ``status``/``reason`` below are the pre-scan placeholders the bus overwrites; they are never what lands on disk when the scan fires.
claims.why: Refers to bus overwriting status/reason, not in this chunk.
